FoundationWho we are and what we want

发布源: Heinrich Böll Stiftung -- Germany | 抓取时间: 2026-11-19

The Heinrich Böll Foundation maintains close ties to the German Green Party (Alliance 90/The Greens) and as a think tank for green visions and projects, we are part of an international network encompassing partner projects in approximately 60 countries.

Heinrich Böll's encouragement of civil society interference in politics is a model for the work of the foundation. Its primary task is political education in Germany and abroad to promote the democratic will, the socio-political commitment and international understanding. It is guided by the basic political values of ecology, democracy, solidarity, and nonviolence. The foundation is particularly interested in the realization of a democratic immigration society as well as gender democracy as a relationship of the sexes that is free of dependence and domination.

In addition, the foundation promotes art and culture as an element of its political educational work and as an expression of social self-understanding. Currently, the study program of the Heinrich Böll Foundation supports about 1.200 students and doctoral candidates with scholarships. The general meeting, consisting of 49 persons, is the supreme decision-making body and chooses a. o. the board.

Presently, the full-time executive board is formed by Dr. Imme Scholz and Jan Philipp Albrecht. The management is held by Steffen Heizmann. The statutes provide for a quotation for women and migrants for the Foundation's bodies and the full-time positions.

item.content:encoded:
Thematic Working Groups

发布源: German Institute for International and Security Affairs of the Stiftung Wissenschaft und Politik (SWP) --Germany | 抓取时间: 2026-11-19

Part of our research in the period 2024 to 2026 will be organised in four working groups. They focus on transversal topics, allowing us to draw together diverse expertise and perspectives from across SWP’s research divisions. These topics embrace fundamental questions of great complexity and political urgency. Our research will explore interconnections, impacts, conflicts of goals and options for action. The transversal topics form part of SWP’s currentframework for research(in German only). In this document SWP outlines issues and challenges facing German foreign and security policy and why and how to address them.

Investigating the current situation and future possibilities for international cooperation in the context of systemic rivalry.

Exploring the options for transforming and enhancing the European security order, and how the transition can best be accomplished.

Investigating the global trend of autocratisation and the challenges this presents for Germany and Europe.

Examining the sweeping changes associated with disruptive economic and technological transformations, and the problems and opportunities this creates for Germany and Europe.

item.description: 网站专栏报告。作者: 智库研究员。这篇智库文章初次发表在Institute for Advanced Sustainability Studies --Germany官方网站上。
item.content:encoded:
Climate Facts Paper: How the Climate Crisis Can Be Solved

发布源: Institute for Advanced Sustainability Studies --Germany | 抓取时间: 2026-11-19

A new fact paper has been published to coincide with the COP31 UN Climate Change Conference in Antalya. Issued by the German Climate Consortium (DKK) and Klimafakten, it summarizes key findings from the social sciences and humanities on how the transition to a climate-friendly society can succeed. In the paper, RIFS Scientific Director and co-author Doris Fuchs argues for expanding climate-friendly infrastructure that would benefit lower income households in particular.

Climate action is currently being held back by new fossil fuel subsidies, the rollback of existing climate measures, and a dearth of media coverage. “We need climate policy that is far more ambitious, reliable in the long term, and designed to make climate-friendly choices easy and attractive,” says Professor Angela Oels, chair of the DKK and professor at the Center for Climate Resilience at the University of Augsburg.

As things stand, it seems unlikely that Germany will achieve climate neutrality by 2045. “But that is no reason to give up,” says Tilman Santarius, professor of social-ecological transformation and managing director of the DKK. “Rather, social science research shows how far societal trends and political and economic conditions need to change — but also how far they can change — if the Paris climate goals are still to be met. The new climate facts paper brings together the wide range of solutions available today.”

item.content:encoded:
New Workbook on Youth Participation in Brandenburg

发布源: Institute for Advanced Sustainability Studies --Germany | 抓取时间: 2026-11-19

How does wanting a better place to meet up turn into a concrete project? How do young people find out who is responsible and where they can have a say? A new workbook helps them work out what they want to change and plan their first steps.

Young people have the right to have a say in decisions that affect their everyday lives and the world around them. Yet they often know too little about their participation rights or the practical ways in which they can put forward their own ideas and concerns. This is where the new German-language workbookJugendbeteiligung – Kommunale Beteiligung in Brandenburg: verstehen, planen und selbst gestalten[Youth participation – Local participation in Brandenburg: Understanding, planning, and shaping it yourself] comes in. It helps young people discover their strengths, put into words what they would like to change, and plan next steps together. For practitioners working with young people, it offers an accessible way to turn everyday experiences and interests into concrete issues to take forward.

Staff from the Research Institute for Sustainability at GFZ (RIFS) and the Brandenburg Competence Centre for Child and Youth Participation (KiJuBB) developed the workbook together with young people from Brandenburg. It explains participation rights in accessible language, encourages reflection, and motivates young people to take action themselves. Many companies struggle to assess the financial risks associated with circular business models in advance. The Circular Economy Business Case Calculator provides businesses with a ready-to-use solution for independently estimating the potential returns from circular business strategies.

发布源: 9. Wuppertal Institute for Climate, Environment and Energy --Germany | 抓取时间: 2026-11-19

How can the desire for greater sustainability be turned into a viable business model? Many companies struggle to assess the financial risks associated with circular business models in advance. This is where the Wuppertal Institute comes in: its Circular Economy Business Case Calculator provides businesses with a ready-to-use solution for independently estimating the potential returns from circular business strategies. Whether it's refurbishment, rental or repair, the free tool enables businesses to compare complex scenarios and identifies the conditions under which the transition makes economic sense.

Wuppertal, 20 October 2026: The circular economy is high on the political agenda in Germany. In early June 2026, the German Federal Cabinet adopted an action programme to implement the National Circular Economy Strategy (NKWS). The scale of the economic potential is illustrated by a May 2026 study by the Federation of German Industries (BDI) and Boston Consulting Group: by 2045, the circular economy could generate an additional €880 billion in value added for German industry.

For individual companies, however, these headline figures often leave a crucial question unanswered: is developing a circular business model financially worthwhile? And if so, when will it start to pay off? Companies considering repair, refurbishment or rental can take encouragement from political support and impressive industry-wide figures, but have few tools available to assess their own business cases.

The escalating climate crisis is increasing the pressure for action in international climate policy. Against the backdrop of the 1.5-degree threshold being set to be exceeded, the 31st Conference of the Parties to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31) must provide key impetus for ambitious emissions reductions and the consistent implementation of existing targets – more urgently than ever. The conference will take place from 9 to 20 November 2026 in Antalya, Turkey.

Wuppertal, 5 November 2026: International climate policy continues to face major challenges: National climate pledges have so far been insufficient to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius. At the same time, geopolitical tensions and crises are hindering cooperation among nations as well as the agreement on and implementation of common goals.

"International climate policy faces the Herculean task of making significantly faster progress despite difficult conditions. The extreme weather events that occurred worldwide in 2026 – whether heat waves or heavy rainfall – have once again made it clear just how urgent the need for action is. Inaction is not an alternative to ambitious climate protection; rather, it causes greater harm to people and the economy – and ultimately to significantly higher economic costs," emphasises Prof. Dr.-Ing. item.content:encoded:
Supporting Max Planck

发布源: 2. Max Planck Institutes --Germany | 抓取时间: 2026-11-19

Our scientists are driven to find answers to the big questions of our times. In tackling their field in scientific frontier research they need courage, talent, persistence - and your unique support!

Excellent frontier research is a high risk mission, requiring high trust, too. The results are at times not predictable, nonetheless this search is what drives us to push forward and exceed boundaries of knowledge. And knowledge is essential for progress: technologies and medical care improve our lives and ensure economic prosperity. Therefore, research in Germany is largely state-funded, because knowledge is a publicly invaluable good.

Nevertheless, public funding alone at times does not suffice, as our scientists find themselves in a tough international competition. Max Planck Society can only stand up to and succeed when donors support our research, too.

Here, our Major Donors, ourSupporting Membersand ourBoards of Trusteesset benchmarks. And because our world class scientists need that extra head room (especially when public funding ist not available), we are generously supported by theMax Planck Foundation.

Excellent frontier research also requires outstanding support. Succeeding as a visionary is part of your set of beliefs.

Join us on this frontier journey - you are in best company.

The ability to use, repair and recycle products for longer depends on one thing above all else: reliable data. A new In Brief from the Wuppertal Institute explains why digitisation is crucial for a functioning circular economy and which role the Circular Economy Information Ecosystem (CEIS) plays within this context.

Wuppertal, 15 April 2026: The transition to a functioning circular economy is one of the key challenges of our time. We can only achieve our climate goals and reduce environmental damage by using resources efficiently and keeping them in circulation. At the same time, the transition to a circular economy is the appropriate response to the intensifying geopolitical tensions and growing dependence on raw materials, which are increasingly shaping the framework conditions for business and industry. Closed-loop systems help make supply chains more resilient. This transformation requires digitisation to succeed. For the circular economy to work in practice, companies, public authorities and other stakeholders must be able to exchange and use data more effectively in future.

In the In Brief titled "The Circular Economy Information Ecosystem: Prerequisite for Success and Driver of Innovation for the Digital Circular Economy", Prof. Dr.-Ing. Stephan Ramesohl and Dr. Holger Berg from the Digital Transformation Research Unit at the Wuppertal Institute outline the digital foundations necessary to achieve this.
